plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the recorded account of the Edgehill phantom battle (Warwickshire, Christmas 1642): two months after the first great battle of the English Civil War, shepherds see the battle fought again in the midnight sky, Kineton's magistrate and minister report it and King Charles sends six officers to disprove it; the twist is that the officers see it too and recognise fallen men they knew, including the king's standard bearer Sir Edmund Verney, and swear to it under oath — tradition says the sightings stopped once the dead were buried.

beats.say: Christmas Eve, 1642, Edgehill: shepherds saw a battle in the sky.
A battle in the sky? Who could be fighting up there?
A true story. Printed in a pamphlet in January 1643.
Two months earlier, on October twenty-third, a real battle raged here.
King Charles against Parliament. The first big battle of England's civil war.
Almost thirty thousand men fought here for about three hours.
And when it was over, who had won?
Nobody, really. And hundreds of men never left this field.
One of them carried the king's own banner, Odo. Remember him.
His name was Sir Edmund Verney. He never came home.
Then came Christmas. A Saturday night, between twelve and one.
Listen. Drums. Far away at first... and coming closer.
Then groans. Clashing armour. Horses. Cannons firing in the dark.
Look up! Two armies! Fighting the same battle again!
Shepherds and travellers stood frozen until two or three in the morning.
They ran to Kineton's magistrate, William Wood, and minister, Samuel Marshall.
Two armies in the sky? Then show us, if it's true.
If it is true, Odo, the dead of Edgehill are still fighting.
Christmas night, it came again. Then a whole week of silence.
Then it returned. Saturday, Sunday. Four hours each time.
Word of it travelled all the way to the king, at Oxford.
King Charles chose six men of his own to find the truth.
Colonel Lewis Kirke, Captain Dudley, Captain Wainman, and three more gentlemen.
We'll see for ourselves what these people really saw.
They waited in the winter cold until the next Saturday night.
At midnight, far off, the drums began again.
There! Two armies... just as they stood in October!
The king's own officers saw the phantom battle with their own eyes.
New true story every day. Subscribe so you never miss one.
Now they must report to the king, Odo. Under oath.
Sunday night they watched again. This time, they saw a face.
That man with the banner. I know him.
They recognised Sir Edmund Verney. The banner bearer who fell in October.
The man who never came home... came back to the field.
Other faces too. Men the officers had known, killed in that battle.
They swore to the king that it was all true.
Then the pamphlet was printed: A Great Wonder in Heaven.
Local tradition says the dead still lying out there were then buried.
And after that, the great battles in the sky stopped.
So all they wanted was to rest?
Visitors still say they hear drums near October twenty-third.
It is often said these are England's only officially recorded ghosts.
Not a campfire legend, Odo. A report written for a king.
My lantern stays here tonight. For the ones who never got home.
Liked this? The sealed Chase Vault story is next on the channel.
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

イングランド・エッジヒルの実際の記録。イングランド内戦最初の大きな戦いから2か月後の1642年のクリスマス、羊飼いたちは夜空で同じ戦いが繰り返されるのを見ました。国王チャールズ1世は自らの士官を調査に送り、1643年の小冊子『A Great Wonder in Heaven』に彼らが見たものが記されています。
